question: Which parts of our color additive petition stay non-public: our manufacturing process, sales figures, and formula?
answer: The requested provisions require that the manufacturing process, sales figures, and formula of the color additive petition remain non-public. The evidence supports this by stating that the petition process for color additives includes information similar to that submitted in food additive petitions, and that the data and information submitted establish safety and suitability. The sources cited are [1].

sources.text: ns 28 As is the case for a food additive, a GRAS regulation reiterates or describes only a small fraction of the information in a GRAS affirmation petition. Likewise, information in our response to a GRAS notice describing a notified substance reiterates or describes only a small fraction of the information in the GRAS notice. E. Petition Process for Listing a Color Additive Our implementing regulation for the color additive petition process is in 21 CFR 71.1. In general, a color additive petition includes information similar to that submitted in a food additive petition (see section A in Appendix 2 of this document). If we find that the data and information submitted in a color additive petition establish that the color additive will be safe and suitable under the conditions of its intended use, we list the use of the color additive through a regulation (21 CFR 70.42(a)). sources.heading: Nutrition labeling of food.
sources.text: (C) Submit a petition, under 21 CFR 10.30, to request an alternative means of compliance. The petition must provide scientific data or other information for why the amount of added sugars in a serving of the product is likely to have a significant reduction in added sugars compared to the amount added prior to non-enzymatic browning and/or fermentation. A significant reduction would be where reduction in added sugars after non-enzymatic browning and/or fermentation may be significant enough to impact the label declaration for added sugars by an amount that exceeds the reasonable deficiency acceptable within good manufacturing practice under paragraph (g)(6) of this section. In addition, the scientific data or other information must include the reason that the manufacturer is unable to determine a reasonable approximation of the amount of added sugars in a serving of their finished product and a description of the process that they used to come to that conclusion.
